posts.title: On the journey from 'CFO' to 'Full Stack'
posts.content:
Hey all 👋.

Came across Parker on YouTube a month ago talking about Task Master. A few videos later it was clear to me he had a finger on the pulse, was focusing on the right things, and was on a similar learning hunt to me.

I've always wanted to write code, but never thought I could manage the learning curve 17 years into a varied career in accounting, cinematography, and business. Then when our developer showed me GPT-3.5 at the end of 2022 I saw I might be wrong (and my imagination was hooked).

2.5 years later AI has written a lot of code, and I have been having SO much fun. Started with scraping, and automations to support some of my roles in my startup (My title is CFO, but I manage everything other than sales and product). I've build a moderately complex Node.js (no UI, haven't got my head around Frontend yet) lead sourcing tool for our outbound cold email campaigns (which brought over a week of SDR work for me down to less than a day). It was my first stab into a db (SQLite). Love poking around in the Network tab and seeing the XHR logs. Chrome extensions for pulling LinkedIn data have been fun too.

Last year I started writing all of our E2E playwright tests for our group learning app to help the team out (we are a small team). Working sudo in our application made me really want to be able to contribute to the codebase, but I knew my knowledge gap would create more headaches for our CTO and Senior Dev than was helpful.

I'm really well up to date with all the models and AI tooling for the job, but I have very low understanding of how any of the TS/JS or Python that AI writes for me actually works.

So, here is my goal for this community. To learn and grow to the point I can start raising PR's for our codebase. I have a lot of Typescript, React, and Node to learn—and will need all the help I can get.

I warmly welcome all the help any of you are kind enough to offer me along the way 🙋‍♂️!

PS - If your curious, my company is called [Makeshapes](https://www.makeshapes.com/).

posts.title: Upgraded YouTube Title Generator using Claude Workbench
posts.content:
You are a skilled content creator tasked with generating clickbait titles. Your goal is to create increasingly attention-grabbing titles based on a given script and draft title.

Here is the script:
<script>
{{SCRIPT}}
</script>

And here is the draft title:
<draft_title>
{{DRAFT_TITLE}}
</draft_title>

Your task is to create 10 titles, each more clickbaity than the last. Follow these steps:

1. Analyze the script and draft title to identify key elements that can be emphasized or exaggerated.
2. Create a list of 10 titles, starting with a mildly clickbaity version and progressively increasing the clickbait factor.
3. Ensure that each title is more attention-grabbing than the previous one.
4. Use common clickbait techniques such as:
- Creating a sense of urgency
- Invoking curiosity
- Using numbers or lists
- Making bold claims
- Using emotional triggers

Before providing your final list of titles, wrap your analysis in <content_analysis> tags. Consider the following:
- List out 5-10 key elements from the script that could be emphasized.
- Brainstorm 3-5 different clickbait techniques and how they could be applied to this content.
- Outline a strategy for escalating clickbait intensity from title 1 to title 10.
- What emotions or reactions are you trying to evoke in potential viewers?

It's OK for this section to be quite long.

After your analysis, present your list of 10 titles in <titles> tags, with each title on a new line and numbered from 1 to 10.

Example output structure (do not use this content, it's just to illustrate the format):

<content_analysis>
\[Your detailed analysis and strategy for creating clickbait titles\]
</content_analysis>

<titles>
1. \[Mildly clickbaity title\]
2. \[Slightly more clickbaity title\]
...
10. \[Extremely clickbaity title\]
</titles>

Now, proceed with your analysis and creation of clickbait titles based on the provided script and draft title.

posts.title: Wordpress Vibe Coding - The why and how
posts.content:
Let me share this here hoping it can benefit you if you are also in my situation. I am well versed in WordPress, Drupal, Laravel and a variety of PHP-based CMSes and systems. My Python skills are 1 or 2 out of 10 at the moment (but rising).

When it comes both coding and learning at the same time, it impairs my speed and confidence in the task at hand. @Parker Rex has shared his thoughts on the topic, especially the need for just-in-time and continuous learning. HOWEVER, THE REALITY IS THAT WE HAVE TO BE PRACTICAL AND GROW AT OUR OWN PACE.

If you have clients who wanted your services now, they may not have the patience to wait for you to learn new programming languages.

Most PHP content management systems have built-in ecosystems, plugins, themes, packages, modules that fit the bill for many client websites. There is no need to re-invent the wheel or redo in Python what is freely available on GitHub.

Many people look down on PHP, but my friend Gemini says "PHP is a dominant force on the internet, with a substantial majority of websites relying on this server-side scripting language. As of early to mid-2025, estimates indicate that PHP is used by approximately 74.5% to 80% of all websites whose server-side programming language is known. Some sources suggest that around 77% to 79% of all websites rely on PHP to some degree.

If you come from the PHP community, there is good news. Actually this may apply to other systems like Shopify or social media accounts but let's focus on PHP systems.

You can have your server support both Python and PHP.... then you can code CLI programs to integrate with the CMS. For example if you want to generate images through AI, it might be better to do it in Python and then sync them with your content from the CLI. You can batch create articles, generate data and add content directly to the CMS database, use webhooks to post, or do API integrations.

Here are some useful resources if you want to take that route:

[https://deepwiki.com/wp-cli/wp-cli](https://deepwiki.com/wp-cli/wp-cli)

posts.title: 🔥🔥 Logical 3 Step PRD Prompt Flow (bind these to !f1, !f2, !f3) No Task Master Needed (but its great)
posts.content:
BEFORE YOU START PASTING PROMPTS READ THIS SNIPPET FROM A PREVIOUS POST:

The P in PRD is product. [I made a whole course on product.](https://www.skool.com/troublefreeai/classroom/4ecde1d9?md=af78606ddf5748449b05dc42937cdef7) If you watch it you'll be better at building product. I tried to make it as anti-snooze as possible.

Product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.

- Narrow the problem- Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem- List things out of bounds (no goes)- List potential rabbit holes (things you know could be a time bomb)- Then time box it as a constraint (less relevant - never tell the AI a time box)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I haven't made videos about this ... but writing it ou,t I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if you've thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase, or where you should start if it's brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once you're in the editor...
because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then it's 4 am and
You're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.
If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, researching tech/designs / other people's repos I can learn from. (use search operators like `language:Typescript <concept_you_want_to_learn`

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

posts.content:
I like parts of cline, parts of claude code, parts of augment... gosh its exhausting how much stuff there is. I want to use 1-3 tools and get GREAT with them. GREAT defined by product with paying customers. I want to pay one provider (cursor) and simplify my workflow.

last week i used every single tool and got caught becoming the tool fiddler

dont be a tool fiddler

posts.title: Make Rules in Cursor As You Build
posts.content:
Similar to how you should clean as you cook in a kitchen, you should clean your codebase and create rules as you're building. These have a compounding effect on the code quality and the joy you'll get from working in your codebase.

Cursor is incredibly powerful because you can start to create rules around how you'd like things done moving forward. You can select the areas of the codebase that you'd like for these rules to apply to.

I want to cover a couple of the different best practices that I found by digging up Cursor Engineers on X

FAQ:
-----------------

What is an .mdc?

| It's just a markdown file with structured frontmatter that we render a custom editor for so you can @-mention files in yoru codebase and to make sure the metadata stays intact.

Michael also mentioned that the “MDC” in the .mdc file extension means “Markdown Cursor”:

| It means “Markdown Cursor” we just needed a unique extension so we could use the custom editor for these but not for regular markdown files.

Creating rules as you go (taken from Task Master).

-----------------

When should I create a new rule?
Introduce rules when you have new patterns that you want to continue throughout the project. For example, querying data, mutating data, writing components, structuring markdown files, doing external API calls, doing logging, doing traces.

Grab the prompt below and store it in your .cursor/rules/cursor_rules.mdc:

```
---
description: Guidelines for creating and maintaining Cursor rules to ensure consistency and effectiveness.
globs: .cursor/rules/*.mdc
alwaysApply: true
---

- **Required Rule Structure:**
```markdown
---
description: Clear, one-line description of what the rule enforces
globs: path/to/files/*.ext, other/path/**/*
alwaysApply: boolean
---

- **Main Points in Bold**
- Sub-points with details
- Examples and explanations
```

- **File References:**
- Use `\[filename\](mdc:path/to/file)` (\[filename\](mdc:filename)) to reference files
- Example: \[prisma.mdc\](mdc:.cursor/rules/prisma.mdc) for rule references

Common issues are:

installing to your GLOBAL cursor AND your project.

posts.title: Prompt for Writing Professional, Short, Business Emails
posts.content:
``` markdown
You are tasked with drafting a professional email based on the provided parameters. Follow these steps carefully to create an effective and appropriate email:

1. First, review the email parameters provided:

<email_parameters>
{{EMAIL_PARAMETERS}}
</email_parameters>

2. Analyze the parameters:
- Identify the recipient type and adjust your language accordingly
- Understand the purpose of the email to focus your content
- Note the required tone to set the appropriate style
- List the key points to ensure all necessary information is included
- Take note of any special requirements

3. Structure your email as follows:
a. Greeting: Use an appropriate salutation based on the recipient type
b. Opening paragraph: Briefly state the purpose of the email
c. Body paragraphs: Address each key point in a clear and concise manner
d. Closing paragraph: Summarize the main message and state any expected actions
e. Sign-off: Use an appropriate closing based on the tone and recipient type

4. When drafting the email:
- Maintain the specified tone throughout the email
- Dont use corporate jargon
- Be optimistic
- Ensure clarity and conciseness in your writing
- Keep it short, make every word fight for its right
- Use professional language and avoid jargon unless appropriate for the recipient
- Proofread for grammar and spelling errors

5. Address special requirements:
- If a deadline is specified, clearly mention it in the email body
- If attachments are needed, list them at the end of the email and ensure to mention them in the body
- If follow-up is required, indicate the next steps or expected response

6. Once you have drafted the email, present it within <email_draft> tags. Include placeholders for any information that would typically be filled in by the sender (e.g., \[Your Name\], \[Your Title\], etc.).

Remember to tailor the email to the specific parameters provided and ensure it achieves its intended purpose while maintaining the appropriate tone and professionalism.
